intro: A smart contract with no interface is just an address most people can't use. A decentralised application — a dApp — is a normal web frontend that talks to a contract instead of a company's server. This lesson shows how that connection works: the libraries that speak to the chain, the crucial difference between reading (free) and writing (a transaction), and how a wallet like MetaMask signs the user's transactions so your site never touches their keys. By the end you'll understand the full path from a button click to an on-chain state change.
objectives: Explain what a dApp is and how its frontend differs from a normal web app
Use a library (ethers.js/viem) with a provider and a signer
Distinguish reading state (a free call) from writing state (a transaction)
Describe the wallet-based flow that keeps user keys off your site

blocks.text: A **dApp** (decentralised application) is, in most cases, an ordinary website — HTML, CSS, JavaScript — whose *backend logic* lives in a smart contract on a public blockchain instead of on a company's servers. The frontend still runs in the user's browser and can be hosted anywhere; what's different is where it sends its important operations. Instead of calling your own API to, say, record a vote, the frontend asks the user's wallet to send a transaction to a contract, and the contract records the vote on-chain. The user's data and the core logic aren't in your control, which is the whole point: the app keeps working even if your website disappears, because the contract is still there.

sections.heading: The library, the provider, and the signer

blocks.text: Your JavaScript can't talk to the blockchain directly; it uses a library — **ethers.js** or **viem** are the popular ones — that speaks the chain's protocol. Two objects from that library matter most. A **provider** is a read-only connection to the chain: with it you can query balances, read contract state, and fetch past events, all for free. A **signer** represents an account that can *authorise* transactions — it's backed by the user's wallet, and using it is what triggers the wallet to pop up and ask the user to confirm. The rule of thumb: **provider to read, signer to write.** You get the signer from the browser wallet the user has connected, so your site can request transactions without ever seeing the private key.

sections.heading: Reading is free; writing is a transaction

blocks.text: This is the distinction that shapes every dApp. **Reading** the chain — calling a `view` function, checking a balance — costs nothing, happens instantly, and needs no wallet confirmation, because you're only querying data every node already has. **Writing** — calling a function that changes state — is a **transaction**: it costs gas, must be signed by the user's wallet, and takes time to be mined and confirmed. So a read returns a value immediately, while a write returns a transaction you then wait on. Designing a dApp is largely about knowing which operations are reads (show them freely, update the UI often) and which are writes (prompt the wallet, show a pending state, wait for confirmation).

The **ABI** (Application Binary Interface) mentioned in the code is the contract's public interface described as data — the list of its functions and events — which the library needs to encode your calls correctly. Your framework produces the ABI when it compiles the contract, so you pass it straight through to the frontend.

sections.heading: The wallet keeps keys off your site

blocks.text: The security model here is elegant and worth appreciating. Your site never asks for, sees, or stores the user's private key. Instead, when your code calls a state-changing function through a **signer**, the request goes to the user's **wallet**, which shows the user exactly what they're about to sign — the contract, the function, the value — and only signs and broadcasts if they approve. Your frontend just prepares the transaction and reacts to the result. This means a malicious or buggy dApp can *ask* for a transaction but can't move funds without the user's explicit, informed consent, and a compromised website still can't steal keys it never had.

The flip side: users must actually read what they sign. A deceptive dApp can request a transaction or a token approval that does more than it appears to. This is why the security lesson matters on both sides — and why teaching users to check the wallet prompt is part of building trustworthy dApps.

Now the whole path connects. The user clicks 'Connect wallet'; your site requests accounts and gets a **signer**. The user clicks a button that changes state; your code calls the contract function through the signer, which prompts the **wallet**; the user confirms; the wallet **signs** and broadcasts the transaction; **nodes** verify it and a **validator** includes it in a **block**; your code was `await`ing the transaction and, once it's confirmed, reads the new state back through the **provider** and updates the UI. Every layer from the earlier lessons — keys, transactions, gas, nodes, consensus — is in that one interaction, now with a friendly button in front of it.

items: Connect: request accounts → get a signer from the wallet.
Read: query state through the provider, free and instant.
Write: call a function via the signer → the wallet prompts the user.
Confirm: the user approves; the wallet signs and broadcasts.
Update: await the transaction, then re-read state and refresh the UI.

blocks.text: That is a complete dApp interaction. The full-stack dApp project in this track builds exactly this — a contract plus a frontend that connects a wallet, reads state, and sends transactions. Next, though, the most important lesson for anyone whose contract will hold value: security.

practice.title: Trace a dApp interaction
steps: Explain how a dApp's frontend differs from a normal web app in where its core logic runs.
Describe the roles of a provider and a signer, and which one you use to read versus write.
Write, in pseudocode, a read of a contract's value and a write that changes it, noting which prompts the wallet.
Explain what the ABI is and why the library needs it.
Walk through the full flow from 'connect wallet' to the UI updating after a confirmed transaction.

focus: A dApp is a normal frontend whose backend logic is a smart contract on a public chain.
A library (ethers.js/viem) speaks the chain's protocol from JavaScript.
Provider = read-only, free, instant; signer = authorises transactions via the wallet.
Reading a view function is free; writing is a gas-costing, signed, mined transaction.
The ABI is the contract's function/event list the library needs to encode calls.
The wallet signs transactions, so your site never touches the user's private key.

items.desc: state is on the public chain
an object to call functions on
the interface the library encodes with

pitfalls: Trying to write state with a provider — you need a signer for transactions.
Expecting a write to return a value instantly; it returns a transaction you must await.
Forgetting the ABI, so the library can't encode calls to the contract.
Assuming reads cost gas — querying view functions is free.
Building a dApp that hides what a transaction does; users must be able to review the wallet prompt.

quiz.q: How does a dApp's frontend differ from a normal web app's?
options: It must be written entirely in the Solidity language
Its core logic runs in a smart contract, not on your servers
It cannot use any HTML, CSS, or JavaScript at all
It has to be hosted on a special blockchain-only host
quiz.explain: A dApp is usually an ordinary web frontend, but its important operations go to a smart contract on a public chain rather than to a company's backend — so it keeps working even if the site disappears.

quiz.q: Which do you use to send a state-changing transaction?
options: A provider, which is a read-only connection
A signer, backed by the user's wallet
The contract's ABI on its own
A block explorer such as Etherscan
quiz.explain: A provider only reads; a signer (backed by the user's wallet) authorises transactions, prompting the user to confirm before anything is signed and broadcast.

quiz.q: What is true of reading a view function from a contract?
options: It costs gas and requires a wallet confirmation
It is free, instant, and needs no wallet prompt
It permanently changes the contract's state
It can only be done by the contract's owner
quiz.explain: Reading queries data every node already holds, so it is free and immediate and needs no signature; only writing (a transaction) costs gas and must be signed.

quiz.q: Why does your dApp never need the user's private key?
options: The key is stored in your website's database instead
The wallet signs transactions and returns only the result
Private keys are not used on Ethereum at all
The blockchain emails a signature to your server
quiz.explain: Your code prepares the transaction and the user's wallet signs it after they approve, so the key never leaves the wallet — a compromised site still can't steal a key it never had.

quiz.q: What is the ABI used for?
options: It stores the user's ether balance for the app
It describes the contract's functions so the library can encode calls
It is the private key needed to deploy the contract
It is the fee paid to connect a wallet to the site
quiz.explain: The ABI is the contract's interface as data — its functions and events — which the library needs to correctly encode calls and decode results.
